Neurology · published research

Epilepsy and status epilepticus

Rodent studies report changes in seizure severity and neuronal injury, but a valproate-combination experiment found benefit with a low dose and worse seizure measures with a high dose. No human PBM study for epilepsy was identified.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Rodent studies report changes in seizure severity and neuronal injury, but a valproate-combination experiment found benefit with a low dose and worse seizure measures with a high dose. No human PBM study for epilepsy was identified.

Summary of the Evidence

The epilepsy category contains 12 unique titles: ten animal research publications and two reviews. The animal publications include eight rat and two mouse reports. Several come from related laboratories and use chemically induced seizures, so the publication total should not be read as ten independent disease models. The reviews summarize preclinical work and do not add patient evidence.

Human and clinical evidence

No human treatment study of PBM for epilepsy or status epilepticus was identified in the mapped category. The available clinical discussion appears in reviews and does not provide direct patient outcomes.

Animal evidence

Rodent studies examine seizure behavior, neuronal injury, synaptic markers and metabolism across several chemically induced seizure models. In one peripubertal-rat study, 808-nm transcranial laser treatment after valproic acid was associated with fewer severe seizures and delayed seizure progression when paired with a low valproate dose. With a higher valproate dose, PBM worsened several seizure measures, including seizure stage or duration (Tsai et al. 2022). Other mouse work reports improved synaptic markers and cognitive outcomes alongside reduced seizure measures, but the different induction models and treatment timing limit direct comparison (Hong et al. 2023).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell or tissue study was identified. Metabolomic, inflammatory and synaptic measurements were embedded in the animal experiments.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Reported protocols include transcranial near-infrared light around 808 nm, brief exposures and treatment timed after seizure induction or drug administration. Other animal reports use different wavelengths, schedules and seizure models. One study's high-dose valproate interaction is a direct reason not to generalize its low-dose combination result to other medication levels. The database does not provide one complete dose specification shared across the animal literature.

Interpretation

The findings justify further mechanistic study of PBM in epilepsy models but do not show that it controls seizures in people. Dose, timing and interactions with antiseizure medication remain unresolved, and the opposite results with different valproate doses make translation particularly uncertain.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for human seizure reduction or long-term control Low within selected animal models
Publications and records12 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

All direct evidence is from animal models, with ten animal publications and two reviews. A valproate-combination study found different results with low and high drug doses, showing why model-specific effects cannot be treated as a clinical dose recommendation. Human safety and seizure outcomes remain untested. Controlled translational studies should clarify dose and medication interactions first.
